howItWorks.title: How It Works
howItWorks.subtitle: Understanding the Pkarr resolution flow
howItWorks.whatIsPkarrDesc1: Pkarr (Public Key Addressable Resource Records) is a system that lets anyone publish DNS records using just an Ed25519 key pair — no domain registrar, no ICANN, no centralized authority. Records are stored on a Distributed Hash Table (DHT), the same peer-to-peer technology used by BitTorrent.
howItWorks.whatIsPkarrDesc2: The public key (encoded as 52 z-base32 characters) acts as the “domain name”, and the DHT acts as the “DNS server”. Anyone with the public key can look up the records — and only the key owner can update them.
howItWorks.problemTitle: The problem: browsers can’t do UDP
howItWorks.problemDesc1: The Pkarr DHT runs on UDP (the same protocol used by BitTorrent’s Mainline DHT). However, web browsers are sandboxed — they can only make HTTP/HTTPS and WebSocket connections. There is no way for JavaScript running in a browser (or a browser extension) to open raw UDP sockets and talk directly to the DHT.
howItWorks.problemDesc2: This is a fundamental limitation of the web platform, not a Pkarr limitation. Native apps and CLI tools can query the DHT directly via UDP, but anything running inside a browser cannot.
howItWorks.solutionDesc1: To bridge this gap, Pkarr uses HTTP relay servers. A relay is a server that participates in the DHT (via UDP, like any other node) and also exposes a simple HTTP API. The browser makes a standard HTTPS request to the relay, and the relay queries the DHT on its behalf and returns the result.
howItWorks.solutionDesc2: Think of it as a translator: the browser speaks HTTP, the DHT speaks UDP, and the relay translates between them.
howItWorks.flowSubtitle: Here is exactly what happens when you resolve a Pkarr key using this extension:
howItWorks.step2Title: The extension sends HTTP requests to relay servers
howItWorks.step3Title: The relay queries the DHT (via UDP)
howItWorks.step4Title: The relay returns the binary payload over HTTP
howItWorks.step5Title: The extension decodes the DNS packet
howItWorks.trustIntro: You might ask: “If the relay is a middleman, can it forge or tamper with the records?”
howItWorks.cannotForgeTitle: Relays can withhold, but not forge
howItWorks.faq1Title: Why not use WebSocket or WebRTC to access the DHT directly?
howItWorks.faq2Title: Is the relay a single point of failure?
howItWorks.faq3Title: Can I run my own relay?
howItWorks.step1Desc: You paste or type a 52-character z-base32 public key into the extension (or use the address bar with pk, right-click, or navigate directly to it). The extension strips any prefix like pubky:// or pk: and validates the key format.
howItWorks.step2Desc1: The extension makes parallel HTTPS GET requests to all configured relay servers. By default, it queries:
howItWorks.step2Desc2: Requests are sent simultaneously for speed and redundancy. The first successful response wins. If one relay is down, others can still respond. Each request has a 15-second timeout.
howItWorks.step3Desc1: This is the key step that happens on the relay server, not in your browser. The relay is a full DHT node that communicates with other nodes on the Mainline DHT using UDP.
howItWorks.step3Desc2: The relay looks up the public key on the DHT, finds the nodes that store the record, and retrieves the signed payload. This is the step your browser cannot do directly — the relay does it for you.
howItWorks.step4Desc: Once the relay has the DHT record, it sends back the raw binary payload to the browser over the same HTTPS connection. This payload has a fixed structure:
howItWorks.step5Desc1: The extension extracts the DNS packet (byte 72 onward) and decodes it using the standard DNS wire format. This gives us a list of DNS records — the same types you’d find in traditional DNS:
howItWorks.step5Desc2: Each record has a type, name (subdomain), value (e.g. an IP address), and a TTL (time to live).
howItWorks.step6Desc: The extension displays all DNS records in a table. If a web-navigable record is found (HTTPS, SVCB, A, AAAA, or CNAME pointing to a website), a “Visit Website” button appears. If the key was entered via the address bar, the extension can auto-redirect you to the website.
howItWorks.httpsExplainer: HTTPS — Standard web request. Your browser can do this. The relay receives the request and translates it.
howItWorks.udpExplainer: UDP — Raw DHT protocol. Your browser cannot do this. The relay does it on your behalf.
howItWorks.signedDesc: Every DHT record includes a 64-byte Ed25519 signature made by the key owner’s private key. The relay forwards this signature as-is. A client can verify that the record was indeed published by the owner of the public key and was not modified in transit.
howItWorks.redundancyDesc: The extension queries multiple relays in parallel. If one relay is down, censored, or malicious, the others can still serve the correct record. You can also configure your own relay servers.
howItWorks.cannotForgeDesc: A malicious relay could refuse to return a record (censorship), but it cannot forge a valid record without the owner’s private key. Using multiple relays mitigates the censorship risk.
howItWorks.faq1Answer: The Mainline DHT protocol is UDP-based and the existing network of millions of nodes only speaks UDP. WebSocket and WebRTC require the other end to support them. You’d need a separate overlay network of DHT nodes that support browser protocols, which doesn’t exist today and would be a separate (much smaller) network. HTTP relays are the pragmatic solution — they work today with the existing DHT.
howItWorks.faq2Answer: Not a single point — the extension uses multiple relays and queries them in parallel. Anyone can run a relay, so the set of available relays is open and decentralized. The relay code is open-source.
howItWorks.faq3Answer: Yes! The Pkarr relay software is open-source. You can run your own instance and add its URL to the extension’s relay settings. This gives you full control over your resolution path.
howItWorks.faq4Answer: z-base32 is a human-friendly encoding for binary data. It uses a 32-character alphabet (ybndrfg8ejkmcpqxot1uwisza345h769) designed to avoid visually ambiguous characters. A 32-byte Ed25519 public key encodes to exactly 52 z-base32 characters.
howItWorks.faq5Answer: The Mainline DHT is the distributed hash table used by BitTorrent. It has millions of active nodes worldwide and has been running reliably since 2005. Pkarr leverages this existing infrastructure to store and retrieve signed DNS records without needing its own network.
